CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and hypoxia in HCC -> activation of HIF-1α -> upregulation of ENTPD2 expression in tumor cells -> conversion of extracellular ATP to 5’ AMP -> recruitment and accumulation of MDSCs in the tumor microenvironment -> suppression of CTL activity and immune evasion
Hypothesis: Pharmacological inhibition of ENTPD2 in hepatocellular carcinoma will reduce MDSC-mediated immunosuppression, thereby restoring cytotoxic T cell activity and enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Abstract: This review synthesizes current understanding of the tumor immune microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), highlighting the roles of hypoxia, HIF‐1α, and downstream effectors in promoting immunosuppressive cell populations. Recent evidence suggests that hypoxia-induced activation of HIF‐1α in HCC cells upregulates the enzyme ENTPD2, which converts extracellular ATP into 5′ AMP. This metabolic conversion fosters the recruitment and accumulation of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which in turn attenuate cytotoxic T lymphocyte activity and contribute to immunotherapy resistance. Building on these insights, we propose a novel hypothesis targeting the metabolic crosstalk between hypoxic signals and immune suppression by inhibiting ENTPD2, thereby blunting MDSC recruitment, restoring T cell function, and ultimately enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions.
